claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation in FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers under sustained creep loading is predominantly governed by the yield-strength mismatch between the FCC and BCC layers.
Severe lattice distortion and short-range order amplify the effect of the FCC/BCC yield-strength mismatch.
The yield-strength mismatch localizes dislocation accumulation at FCC/BCC interfaces.
Localized dislocation accumulation activates interface-mediated diffusion processes.
The starting coating retains a nanoscale nanolaminate structure of alternating FCC and BCC high-entropy-alloy layers.
The starting multilayer exhibits pronounced lattice distortion and short-range-order effects.
A temperature window exists that is below nanolaminate destabilization yet high enough to permit diffusion activity.
FCC/BCC interfaces mediate plastic-strain accumulation through dislocation pile-up and enhanced diffusion.
Compositional complexity causes the FCC and BCC layers to exhibit different yield-stress responses.
Under sustained creep loading, dislocations accumulate at interfaces where the yield mismatch is greatest.
Lattice distortion and short-range order exacerbate localized stress concentrations at the interfaces.
Localized interfacial stress concentrations promote diffusion processes that accommodate plastic strain and produce progressive deformation.
HEA multilayers will exhibit a higher creep-strain rate than conventional metallic multilayers under comparable conditions.
Plastic strain in HEA multilayers will be more strongly localized near interfaces than in conventional metallic multilayers.
Deformation will begin elastically and then transition to localized plastic flow.
Conventional metallic multilayers deform more uniformly and with less interface localization because they exhibit weaker lattice-distortion and short-range-order effects.
The proposed mechanism may cease to apply if elevated temperature or prolonged loading destabilizes or substantially alters the nanolaminate architecture.
